title: IELTS Speaking — Practice Test 10
topics: Waiting a long time for something
Patience and the pace of life

questions: Would you describe yourself as a punctual person, or do people end up waiting for you?
What do you usually do when you're stuck waiting — in a queue, at a station, anywhere?
Why do you think being late bothers some people so much and others not at all?
Were you better or worse at being on time when you were younger?
Do you think people in your country will become more punctual or less in the years ahead?
Do you actually enjoy shopping, or is it just something that has to be done?
When you buy something, do you decide quickly or take your time comparing?
What kinds of things do you still prefer to buy in a physical shop rather than online? Why those?
Is the way you shop very different from how your family shopped when you were a child?
Do you think physical shops will still matter in twenty years, or will almost everything move online?

part2.title: Describe an occasion when you had to wait a long time for something.
bullets: where you were and who you were with
how long you had to wait
what you did while you were waiting
part2.explain: and explain how you felt about the wait, and whether what you were waiting for was worth it in the end.
followups: Would you wait that long again for the same thing?
Do you handle waiting better now than you did then?
Is there anything you're waiting for at the moment?

part3.q: Ordering something online and getting it the same day has become normal in many cities. How does that kind of speed change what people expect from the rest of life?
followups: Does the expectation spill over into areas where speed isn't possible?
Is there any way back once people are used to it?

part3.q: Are people today genuinely less patient than earlier generations, or does every generation just say that about the next one?
followups: What evidence would settle the question either way?
What did your grandparents have to wait for that you don't?

part3.q: In some countries people queue in silence for an hour without complaint; in others, a queue is a negotiation. What do you think explains those differences?
followups: What are queues like in your country?
Does how a society queues tell you anything deeper about it?

part3.q: Do you think queue-jumping is a serious wrong, or a trivial one?
followups: Why does it provoke so much anger compared with other small offences?
Are there situations where jumping a queue is justified?

part3.q: Many apps are openly designed so that you never have to wait, or even pause. What effect might that engineering have on people's attention over time?
followups: Is that the app makers' responsibility, or the users'?
Have you noticed any effect on your own attention?

part3.q: Is patience a skill you can train, or a temperament you're simply born with?
followups: Has anything in your life made you more patient?
If it can be trained, whose job is it to train it in children?

part3.q: Some people say waiting for something is half the pleasure of getting it. Is anticipation really worth that much?
followups: Can you think of something that was better because you waited?
Does instant availability make things feel cheaper somehow?

part3.q: Slow travel, slow food, digital detox holidays — slowing down is now something people pay for. What does that say about modern life?
followups: Isn't it odd that slowness has become a product?
Who gets left out when slowing down costs money?

part3.q: Hospitals, courts and visa offices still make people wait months or years. Is some waiting simply unavoidable, or is it always a sign of a system failing?
followups: Does knowing why you're waiting change how the wait feels?
Should people be able to pay to skip these queues?

part3.q: If technology eventually removes almost all waiting from daily life, do you think people will be happier for it?
followups: What might be quietly lost along with the waiting?
Would you take that deal yourself?

fc: Sustains a story where, by definition, not much happens — the two minutes are carried by feelings, small details and time markers, not by plot.
Uses time expressions to keep the narrative moving: "an hour in", "by early afternoon", "just when we'd given up".
In Part 3, connects everyday experience (queues, deliveries) to abstract ideas (expectation, attention) without losing the thread.
Develops answers unprompted — states a view, gives the why, offers a case — so the examiner's prompts stay in reserve.
Pauses to think sound like thinking ("hmm, patience as a skill… I'd say partly") and are followed by fluent stretches, not fragments.
lr: Rich waiting-and-time vocabulary: hang around, kill time, drag on, in the meantime, endless, at a standstill, worth the wait.
Shopping and consumer language used precisely: impulse buy, browse, refund, next-day delivery, brick-and-mortar shops, window shopping.
Abstract Part 3 range: instant gratification, anticipation, attention span, convenience culture — deployed for meaning, not decoration.
Natural collocations — "test my patience", "jump the queue", "lose track of time" — with no invented pairings.
Nuance between near-synonyms: patient vs passive, slow vs unhurried, waiting vs procrastinating.
gra: Past continuous and past perfect frame the wait naturally: "we'd been standing there for three hours when the gates finally opened."
Duration structures accurate and varied: "it took ages", "for the best part of a day", "not until midnight did we…" for emphasis.
Present perfect for trends in Part 3: "expectations have shifted", "queuing culture has been eroded by apps."
Conditionals for the speculative questions: "if nobody ever had to wait, anticipation would disappear along with the queues."
Long sentences land their endings; small errors are rare and repaired without derailing the answer.
pron: Clearly intelligible throughout; the boredom, frustration and relief of the story are audible in the voice, not just claimed in words.
Stress carries the evaluative contrasts this test invites: "the wait was awful — the concert was worth every minute."
Elongation and pace used expressively: "it dragged o-o-on" delivered slowly actually demonstrates the meaning.
Multi-syllable topic words — anticipation, gratification, inevitable, temperament — stressed on the right syllable.
Question-final intonation natural on rhetorical turns ("and was it worth it? honestly, yes") without sounding theatrical.

band9.part1: Direct answer first, then a reason or a true small detail — two to four sentences, never one word. For "What do you usually do when you're stuck waiting?" a Band 9 answer owns its ordinariness: "Honestly? Phone, like everyone else. Though if the battery's gone I people-watch, and I've started to think I prefer it — a railway platform is better theatre than most series." It answers, admits, and adds a view — all in natural spoken rhythm.
part2: Open with the object of the wait — say immediately what you were waiting for and roughly when this was ("two years ago, outside a ticket window, for a concert I'd waited half my life to see").

Set the scene — where you were, who was with you, and one physical detail that makes it real: the heat, the plastic chairs, the man ahead of you with a folding stool who clearly knew something you didn't.
Mark the time passing — walk through the wait in stages rather than as one block: the confident first hour, the doubtful third, the point where leaving felt as costly as staying.
Fill the middle honestly — the third and fourth bullets want texture: the games played, the rumours passed down the queue, the friendship struck up with strangers you never saw again.
Deliver the ending — the moment the wait ended, described at half speed; after minutes of nothing happening, this is where the story pays off, so give it detail.
Answer the verdict directly — was it worth it? Say yes or no plainly, then one sentence on what the wait itself gave you or cost you, which answers the explain line completely.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: Are people today genuinely less patient than earlier generations, or does every generation just say that about the next one?
framework: Answer: commit with nuance — e.g. both are true: the complaint is ancient, but this time the environment really has changed.

Explain: give the mechanism — patience is partly a habit formed by what daily life demands, and daily life now demands almost none: food, entertainment and answers all arrive in seconds, so the muscle gets no exercise.

Example: one concrete contrast — my grandmother waited three weeks for a letter from her brother and thought nothing of it; I've watched people give up on a video because it buffered for five seconds.

Alternative view: concede genuinely — Roman writers complained about impatient youth, and every technology from trains to telegrams was accused of destroying patience, so some of this is just the oldest complaint wearing new clothes.
Evaluate: land the judgement — the grumbling is recycled, but the buffering test is real and measurable, so I'd say this generation isn't worse by nature — it's simply never been made to practise.

mistakes.title: Choosing a five-minute wait
mistakes.detail: "I waited twenty minutes for my food to be delivered" cannot carry a two-minute story. Pick a wait with real duration — a visa, exam results, a queue that ate a whole day — so the middle bullets have something to hold.

mistakes.title: Skipping the 'what you did while waiting' bullet
mistakes.detail: It looks like the boring bullet, but it's where the story lives: the conversations, the games, the slow negotiation with boredom. Candidates who skip it end up with thirty seconds of content and ninety of silence.

mistakes.title: Announcing feelings instead of showing them
mistakes.detail: "I felt very bored and frustrated" is a label. "By the fourth hour I'd read every poster on that wall twice" is the same feeling, worth more, and takes no extra vocabulary.

mistakes.title: No verdict on whether it was worth it
mistakes.detail: The explain line asks a direct question and examiners notice when it goes unanswered. End with a plain 'worth it' or 'not remotely worth it' and one sentence of why.

mistakes.title: Turning every Part 3 answer into an anti-phone lecture
mistakes.detail: "Nowadays people are always on their phones" fits half the questions here and answers none of them well. The questions are about expectations, queues and attention — engage with the specific mechanism, not the general complaint.

mistakes.title: Moralising about impatient young people
mistakes.detail: "The new generation wants everything immediately" is a complaint, not an analysis. The generations question explicitly offers the counter-view — that every era says this — and Band 8–9 candidates take that bait and weigh it.

mistakes.title: One-word Part 1 shopping answers
mistakes.detail: "Do you enjoy shopping?" — "Not really." The examiner can't award fluency to silence. Add the because and the exception: "Not really, unless it's bookshops — I can lose an afternoon in one of those."

mistakes.title: Reciting online-vs-offline shopping essays
mistakes.detail: The comparison is a coursebook classic, and memorised advantage-disadvantage lists surface immediately. Anchor answers in your own actual habits — what you genuinely still buy in person, and why.

mistakes.title: Monotone delivery of a story about boredom
mistakes.detail: A flat voice describing a long wait is doubly flat. This cue card is an invitation to use pace and stress expressively — the slow 'it dragged on' — and pronunciation marks reward exactly that.

mistakes.title: Treating 'patience: skill or temperament?' as either/or
mistakes.detail: Picking one word and defending it to the death misses the interesting ground. The strong answer names what's inborn, what's trainable, and what kind of life does the training — then commits to where the balance lies.
